extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and students of fiction craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing between dramatic (scene-based) and pictorial/narrative (background-description) methods in novel writing — when to let action speak, when to supply setting, and how to balance them to serve character, credibility, and unity. Draws on examples (Balzac, Dickens, Stevenson) to illustrate when to amplify or restrain drama with setting and presentation mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the issue emerge through the situation (show, don't tell)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To see the issue slowly unfolding and flowering out of the middle of a situation, and to watch it emerge unaided, with everything that it has to say said by the very lines and masses of its structure' — prefer that the story’s meaning be enacted in action and structure rather than poured out by an explanatory authorial spokesman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the 'spokesman' who 'pours out his information' and 'talks and talks' about a subject that might be revealing itself without him. Strive for drama/scene that conveys meaning; silence or minimise intrusive exposition unless strictly necessary. Anti-pattern: over-authorial commentary that tells the reader what to think rather than letting scenes show it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a dramatic motive when the story suits it
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A novelist prefers a dramatic motive, and might cast it into a round, sound action and leave it in that form if he chose.'  When a story is essentially action-driven, entrust its development to enacted scenes and dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama is 'paramount' for placing and establishing a piece of action; it gives direct force and validity. There is 'plenty of room for enterprise and experiment' in choosing a purely dramatic form when the subject allows. Score dramatic immediacy highly when the heart of the story lies in action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize drama’s limitation in conveying background and associations
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The dramatic scene is vivid and compact; but it is narrow, it can have no great depth, and the colour of the atmosphere can hardly tell within the space.'  Strict drama is at a disadvantage in expressing the outlying associations and broad background of a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the dramatic presentation is not supplemented by a wider survey or pictorial narration, the story's background and social atmosphere may fail to make their full impression. Use broader narrative perspective where depth, context, and the life behind the action are essential. Anti-pattern: relying solely on staged scenes to convey complex social or historical atmospheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe setting clearly when the background is particular and essential
rubrics_metrics.description: 'For the purposes of her story it is important that her setting should be clearly seen and known... Nanda’s world is not the kind of society that can be taken for granted.'  When a story depends on a very specific or artificial background, make that setting explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If characters’ behaviour depends on a singular milieu, do not assume readers will infer it; render the setting by whatever means needed so characters are 'rendered' and the situation understood. Henry James sometimes implied setting successfully, but where specificity matters, prefer clear pictorial description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the pictorial/generalized picture to support and propel drama
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The effect of the generalized picture, supporting the play of action, is one in which Balzac particularly delights... it becomes a kind of propulsive force applied to the action at the start.'  Massed, pictorial depiction can prepare and energise the ensuing drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Massing background details and impressions beforehand can create a reserve of vigour that helps the action when it comes. Examples: Balzac’s Maison Vauquer preparing the tale of Goriot. Use pictorial set-up deliberately to lend weight and plausibility to later dramatic events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make setting economical — supply character and energy, not mere decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Balzac’s care in creating the scene... is truly economical; it is not merely a manner of setting the stage for the drama, it is a provision of character and energy for the drama when it begins.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you describe place, do so because those details will actively serve the action or illuminate character. Well-chosen environment details should carry into and enrich the drama rather than remain ornamental. Anti-pattern: lavish description that does not contribute to character, motive, or plot momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let irrelevant cross-book associations disturb a single story’s unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who carry 'their lengthening train of old associations from book to book' may add unity to a vast scheme, but 'in any single story, such of these people as appear by the way... must for the time being shed their irrelevant life; if they fail to do so, they disturb the unity of the story and confuse its truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In an individual novel, ensure minor/recurring characters only bring the information that matters to the foreground action. Prior knowledge from other works should not introduce distracting, irrelevant backstory that weakens focus or confuses the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial art to tone down or confirm incredible or extravagant drama
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Where the action... is likely to seem harsh, overcharged, romantic, it is made to look less so, less hazardous and more real, by recourse to the art of the picture-maker.'  Pictorial background can extenuate and thus make an otherwise implausible climax credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a dramatic plot risks seeming overwrought or unbelievable, embed it in a believable, well-drawn world so the contrast is softened and the reader accepts the event. Balance is crucial: Balzac sometimes failed because romance clashed too sharply with sober detail; Dickens often succeeded in merging the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce violent or romantic climaxes gradually within a credible, populated scene
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The chief characteristic... is this careful introduction of violent drama into a scene already prepared to vouch for it — a scene so alive that it compels belief, so queer that almost anything might happen there naturally.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a broad, believable milieu — populated with characters and small incidents — before concentrating the plot into sudden, intense action. Dickens’s method (e.g., Bleak House) models how to approach a coloured climax cautiously so it feels earned rather than dumped in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that scene-based presentation often forces sharply defined (crystallized) characters
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Because Dickens is always readier to work in action and dialogue... he is forced to crystallize and formulate his characters very sharply... he is so often reduced to the expedient of labelling his people with a trick or a phrase.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on immediate scenes and dialogue rather than extended, panoramic narration, be prepared to render characters in sharper, more concentrated form — memorable gestures, repeated traits, or concise labels — so they register quickly within limited scenes. Anti-pattern: expecting broad, subtle social sketches from short scene appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose narrative mode (person/presentation) to tilt the book towards drama or picture
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The value of rendering it as somebody’s narrative... is the value of working the drama into a picture, of passing it through a man’s thought and catching his reflection of it.'  First-person or chosen narrative mode can either dramatize or pictorialise depending on subject and aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match voice and mode to desired effect: first-person can dramatize (being on the spot) or serve as a framed pictorial impression; decide whether the narrator’s presence will heighten action or tone it into reflection. Examples: Stevenson’s use of first-person in The Master of Ballantrae (drama) vs Esmond (pictured narrative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise and full about physical surroundings when they are integral to the story
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Balzac... cannot think of his people without the homes they inhabit... he is so sure that every detail must be known... down to the vases on the mantelpiece or the pots and pans in the cupboard.'  When setting is integral, supply minute, business-like detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character’s life and behaviour are rooted in a particular environment, render that environment concretely and insistently so the reader accepts it as the basis for action. Caveat: the text also warns of Balzac’s occasional excess — 'description for its own sake' that becomes tiresome — so include detail only insofar as it serves the book’s truth and action.
